newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Zedillo challenged over election money.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zedillo challenged over election money.

text.p: Mexico's main opposition party returned a $3.7 million campaign funds cheque to the government on Thursday, accusing President Ernesto Zedillo of wasting money on politics instead of helping the poor.

Felipe Calderon Hinojosa, president of the conservative National Action Party (PAN), told reporters the government was spending an exorbitant amount on campaign funding for this year's key congressional elections.

In the teeth of fierce opposition, Zedillo's PRI railroaded a bill through Congress last year giving parties a total of $308 million in campaign funds for key congressional and governors' races this July. The PRI gets the lion's share.
Calderon said the PAN refused to take all of the money and called on other parties, including Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), to hand back the excess.
"The National Action Party believes that this waste is not justifiable or acceptable while the majority of the population live in poverty", Calderon told reporters at the Federal Treasury.

"Financing for political parties and the cost of election organization (in Mexico) is ... three times the public spending on presidential electoral campaigns in the United States, which has three times more electors and a per capita income more than 10 times higher than Mexicans."

Underlining his words, Calderon handed a treasury official a cheque for 29.1 million pesos ($3.7 million) which he said represented the excessive public funding given to his party for the months of November and December.
"With the amount we are handing over today, approximately 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) of street lighting could be installed (or) schoolrooms for 17,120 pupils built," he said.

Calderon told Reuters his party intended to return a total of more than 200 million pesos ($25.6 million) in excessive government funding during the campaign for July 6 elections to choose six state governors, congressional deputies, a quarter of the Senate and the mayor of Mexico City.
The government has awarded the PAN a total of 600 million pesos ($77.1 million), far less than Zedillo's PRI, Calderon said.
PRI officials have said they will take all the money because they want their funding to be transparent, avoiding the risk of being "blackmailed by business or infiltrated by drug traffickers".
A PRI spokesman could not say on Thursday exactly how much the party would take.
The other main opposition party, the PRD, has already announced plans to give the excess of the campaign funds to social projects such as building schools and hospitals.
